draft.title: Language modes in Unit 3
card: A mode is the way a piece reaches its audience: it is read, heard or watched. The mode shapes how the writer builds the piece.
The reader controls the pace and can reread. Writers can use longer sentences, paragraphs, layout and punctuation to guide meaning.
The listener cannot go back. Writers use short sentences, repetition, signposting and rhythm, and the speaker adds pace, tone and pauses.
Meaning comes from images, movement, sound and words together. Writers choose what the audience sees as well as what they are told.
draft.remember: The mode a piece is made for changes how the writer structures it and makes meaning.

a.q: Why might a speech to be heard repeat its main point in different words?
opts: Listeners cannot reread, so repetition helps them follow
Listeners can reread, so repetition shows the layout
Repetition replaces the need for a clear structure
Repetition lets the speaker avoid using tone and pauses
a.why: A listener hears the speech once and cannot go back, so repeating a main point helps it stay clear. The option about rereading is wrong because rereading belongs to a piece that is read.
a.clue: Think about what a listener cannot do.

b.q: Priya turns her written essay on a bushfire into a short film. Which change best suits the new mode?
opts: Show the burnt street in an image instead of describing it
Add long paragraphs so viewers can reread the argument
Add headings and punctuation to guide each viewer's pace
Keep every sentence unchanged and read it aloud in full
b.why: In a watched piece, images carry meaning with words and sound, so showing the street can do the work of a description. Long paragraphs, headings and punctuation suit a piece that is read. Reading the essay aloud unchanged ignores the new mode.
b.clue: In a film, what can the audience see instead of being told?

a.best: Listeners cannot reread, so repetition helps them follow

b.best: Show the burnt street in an image instead of describing it
